title: Alef
hookLine: a silent letter; the rabbis note the Ten Words begin with it (anochi)
last: KAVANAH: SLOW WORDS, A LISTENING HEART.

lines: IT BEGINS WITH A SILENT LETTER.
cards: A mountain wrapped in smoke. Thunder, lightning, the sound of a horn growing louder and louder. The people stand at the foot of Sinai, shaking.
Then God speaks. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, the first words are "I am the LORD thy God." In Hebrew the very first word is anochi, I am.
And anochi begins with alef, the first letter of the alphabet, which on its own makes no sound at all. All that thunder, and the first word opens on a silent letter.

teach.b: You met a small alef once, written small at the start of Leviticus; today, alef itself. First, the sound that isn't there. Alef has no sound of its own.
It holds a place: whatever vowel is written with it, ah or eh or oh, that's what you hear.
It's the open mouth before the word. Second, a midrash. The Torah's first word, bereshit, in the beginning, starts with bet, the second letter.
So an old midrash has alef come before God and complain: I'm the first letter, and you began the world with bet? And God answers: wait. When I give the Torah at Sinai, I will begin with you.
The Ten Words do open with anochi, with alef. The silent letter was saved for the moment of revelation. Third, later teachers.

Some pushed the thought further: they asked what the people at Sinai could really bear to hear, and suggested that perhaps it was the alef alone, the silent opening before any word, and that was enough.

It's a teaching, not a claim about history, but it gives silence an honored place at the mountain. Fourth, an ordinary day. Talk often rushes past the alef; people start speaking before they've finished listening.
Alef sits at the head of the alphabet as a reminder that the breath before the word comes first.
Before bet and every letter after it, there's a letter you can see and cannot hear.

how: Jewish learners meet alef first, as a silent letter that carries its vowel; the rabbis teach that the Ten Commandments open with anochi, 'I am', which begins with alef.

games.q: you're alef, first in the alphabet, and God has just begun the world with bet. in the midrash, what do you do?
o: complain to God that you were passed over.
games.why: alef complains, and God promises: when I give the Torah at Sinai, I'll begin with you. anochi.

practice: Let your mouth fall slightly open, the way it does just before a word, and stay right there at the opening without saying anything.
When a thought arrives, let it pass like a sound in another room, and come back to the open mouth and the breath moving through it. If you pray, let this silence be the doorway into your prayer.
